title: The sages' own prayers (Berakhot 16b–17a)
hook: a page of personal prayers; one became the Amidah's closing prayer
tomorrow: how can a grown man say he's 'as if unformed'?

segments.voice: Yesterday, David blessing God at every stage of a life: bless, O my soul. Today, the sages' own words.

The notes app on a phone is full of things nobody else will read. Half a poem. A text that never got sent. A sentence written at one in the morning. One page of the Talmud reads like that. The tractate has been talking about the Amidah, the standing prayer, the words everyone shares. Then, without warning, it opens the sages' drafts folder: what each of them said after the shared words were done.
screen: `THE DRAFTS FOLDER.` → `AFTER THE SHARED WORDS.` → `WHAT EACH SAGE SAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the page, in plain words. Rabbi Elazar, finishing his prayer, asked that love and brotherhood, peace and friendship would live among his people. Rabbi Yochanan asked God to look at their shame and see their trouble. Rabbi Alexandri was blunt. Our will is to do Your will, he said, so what stops us? The yeast in the dough, and the rule of foreign kingdoms. Each prayer sounds like the person who said it, pressed out of whatever was weighing on him that day. Then comes Mar, son of Ravina. My God, he said, guard my tongue from evil and my lips from speaking deceit. To those who curse me, let my soul be silent. Open my heart to Your Torah. He's leaning on a psalm: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile." And here's the part to tell a friend tonight. Mar's private words didn't stay private. They now sit in the siddur, the prayer book, at the very end of the Amidah, beginning Elohai netzor: my God, guard. One man's own line, said after the shared words, became shared words. So on this page, the fixed prayer and your own prayer aren't rivals. The sages said the prayer everyone says, then kept going in their own voice.
screen: `ELAZAR: LOVE AND FRIENDSHIP.` · `ALEXANDRI: WHAT STOPS US?` · `MAR: GUARD MY TONGUE.` · `NOW IN THE SIDDUR: ELOHAI NETZOR.` · then, large: `YOUR OWN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write one sentence of your own, the way the sages did once the shared words were done: to God if you pray, or as a plain hope if you don't. Keep it short enough to fold into a pocket.
screen: `A PEN, A SCRAP OF PAPER.` · `ONE SENTENCE OF YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: The sages' own prayers. A page of Berakhot where each sage adds his own words, and one of them, Elohai netzor, ends up in the siddur.
Your line: your own prayer. Mar's private sentence now closes the Amidah. Twelve of fifty in Berakhot.

howItsDone: In the siddur, Elohai netzor follows the Amidah, and the end of the Amidah is a place where a person may add a private request in their own words before stepping back.
